Ben

messages.subject: Re: random number generators in probs
messages.body_plain:
How would I create the rng templates for distributions such as double exponential or inv_chi_square, which are not included in boost/random?

Thanks,
Peter

On Mar 1, 2013, at 3:01 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> [I'm moving this discussion back to stan-dev.  I'm not
> even the best person to help with these issues, but I
> can answer this one.]
>
> On 2/28/13 7:03 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>> Or should it be
>>
>> return exp(mu + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) + (exp(sigma * sigma) - 1) * exp(2 * mu + sigma * sigma) * rng_unit_lognorm();
>>
>> On Feb 28, 2013, at 6:43 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>>
>>> Alright. So lognormal would look like the following?

>>>
>>>    template <class RNG>
>>>    inline double

>>>    lognormal_rng(double mu,

>>>               double sigma,
>>>               RNG& rng) {
>>>      using boost::variate_generator;

>>>      using boost::lognormal_distribution;
>>>      using stan::math::value_of;
>>>      using std::exp;
>>>      variate_generator<RNG&, lognormal_distribution<> >
>>>        rng_unit_lognorm(rng, lognormal_distribution<>());
>>>      return exp(mu + sigma * rng_unit_lognorm());
>>>    }
>
> Not quite.  Check out the Wikipedia page:
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution
>
> section "Generating log-normally distributed random variates".
>
> Your scaled and relocated exponential transform would be right
> for an underlying normal distribution (i.e., replace
> lognormal_distribution<> with normal_distribution<>).
>
> You can probably feed the parameters into the lognormal_distribution
> in Boost and not do the scaling yourself.  It might make sense to
> do that in the regular normal distribution, too.
>
> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/doc/html/boost/random/lognormal_distribution.html
>
> It looks like you can just do the following, which is
> probably a better idea in general than trying to code our
> own versions:

>
>     template <class RNG>
>     inline double

>     lognormal_rng(double mu,

>                double sigma,
>                RNG& rng) {
>       using boost::variate_generator;

>       using boost::lognormal_distribution;
>       variate_generator<RNG&, lognormal_distribution<> >
>         lognormal_rng(rng, lognormal_distribution<>(mu,sigma));
>       return lognormal_rng();
>     }
>
> This actually cleans up a bunch of the includes.  The
> value_of shouldn't be included in the normal case, either,
> if you could clean that up.
>
>
> - Bob

>
>>> On Feb 28, 2013, at 5:34 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>
>>>> Peter:
>>>>
>>>> I'd start with the univariate continuous distributions,
>>>> which live in:
>>>>
>>>> src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous
>>>>
>>>> This work should be done on the main branch unless you'd
>>>> be more comfortable working on your own branch.  The reason
>>>> I suggest the main branch is that unlike the fvar stuff,
>>>> these being incomplete won't break the model compilation.
>>>>
>>>> If you do want to keep working in fvar, you should merge
>>>> the master branch into fvar first so that you're reasonably
>>>> up to date with stan/prob.
>>>>
>>>> There's currently a single example implementation in:
>>>>
>>>> src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal.hpp
>>>> ------------------------------------------------------------
>>>>   template <class RNG>
>>>>   inline double
>>>>   normal_rng(double mu,
>>>>              double sigma,
>>>>              RNG& rng) {
>>>>     using boost::variate_generator;
>>>>     using boost::normal_distribution;
>>>>     using stan::math::value_of;
>>>>     variate_generator<RNG&, normal_distribution<> >
>>>>       rng_unit_norm(rng, normal_distribution<>());
>>>>     return mu + sigma * rng_unit_norm();
>>>>   }
>>>>
>>>> where RNG is the templated out type of the basic random number
>>>> generator.  The use of a reference type ("RNG&") in the variate_generator
>>>> is critical in order to advance the shared random number generator we're
>>>> going to use.
>>>>
>>>> This implementation samples from a Normal(0,1) distribution then
>>>> scales by multiplying by sigma (the scale parameter) and relocates
>>>> by adding mu (the location parameter).
>>>>
>>>> Boost supplies many of the basic distributions and the Wikipedia
>>>> has pretty good descriptions of how to sample from the various
>>>> distribtuions.
>>>>
>>>> I'm not sure how best to test these.  The current test is rather
>>>> weak, to say the least:
>>>>
>>>> src/test/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_tes.cpp
>>>> ----------------------------------------------------------------
>>>> TEST(ProbDistributionsNormal, random) {
>>>> boost::random::mt19937 rng;
>>>> EXPECT_NO_THROW(stan::prob::normal_rng(2.0,1.0,rng));
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> Anyone have any suggestions?  We could draw thousands of samples
>>>> and then make sure the sample-based estimates are within the
>>>> sampling variance at a very high threshold (so we don't create
>>>> a lot of false positive tests).  We can also do things like
>>>> test that the output is finite and appropriately signed (e.g.,
>>>> gamma variates should be positive, uniform variates shold be
>>>> constrained between their endpoints, etc.)
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>
>>
>>

messages.body_plain:
You need to figure out how to sample from them.
Usually, you can just transform other distributions.

For instance, the double exponential is aka "Laplace
distribution", and a method of sampling from it is
described here:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_distribution

in the section "Generating random variables according to
the Laplace distribution"

The inverse chi square is an inverse transform.  I
don't see a Wikipedia how to generate example, but I'm
sure you can find it somewhere.  Or you can work it
out from scratch.  I'd suggest reading the transformations
section of the manual (near the back), that explains the
basics.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 3/1/13 2:57 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> Thanks. So how would I implement the chi-squared goodness of fit test that Ben suggested?

How familiar are you with basic hypothesis testing?
It's not that complex mathematically, but can get confusing
conceptually with all the philosophy, and mathematical
details and side conditions.  If looking at the refs below
isn't enough, we can implement one next week.

I'll also build in the code generator so we can plug these
in to the release after next for Stan.

Here's some background, and feel free to bring up questions.

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodness_of_fit

Specifically, Ben's suggesting a chi-squared test

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson%27s_chi-squared_test

For continuous distributions (and for unbounded
or large discrete distributions), you have to bin the
output using the cumulative distribution function.

Here's a nice walkthrough of an example for the normal.

   http://courses.wcupa.edu/rbove/Berenson/10th%20ed%20CD-ROM%20topics/section12_5.pdf

The trick is then adjusting the chi-squared test for the
degrees of freedom, which will be just 1 for us, because we'll
know the parameters from which we were supposed to have
generated the samples (the other degrees of freedom come from
having to estimate those from the data).

The code will need inverse CDFs, for which you can use the
quantile functions from Boost, for example, the normal:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/dist/dist_ref/dists/normal_dist.html

I don't think this will work, by the way, for the Cauchy,
which doesn't have finite means or variances.

- Bob

>
>>
>>   double chi = 0;
>>   double expect [5] = {200, 200, 200, 200, 200};
>>
>>   for(int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
>>     chi += ((bin[j] - expect[j]) * (bin[j] - expect[j]) / expect[j]);
>>
>>   EXPECT_TRUE(chi < 9.49);
>> }
>>
>> I believe the degrees of freedom should be n-1 where n is the number of "bins". Is there a more efficient way to do this?
>
> Right.  You'd normally then add the number of
> free parameters estimated in the goodness of
> fit test, but here we know the parameters.  So
> it's just number of cells minus 1 (the minus 1 is
> because they're constrained to add up, so once
> you know K-1 of them, you know what the Kth is).
>
> > Also, how do I provide a formula for the chi-square value, instead of just 9.49.
>
> The value you want is the quantile (inverse CDF) for the
> chi-square distribution for a quantile like 1 - 1e-6
> where we won't get too many false positives in the tests.
> To do this, you want to use the complementary quantile functions
> because the regular quantiles are arithmetically unstable for values
> close to 1.
>
> See:
>
> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/dist/dist_ref/nmp.html#math_toolkit.dist.dist_ref.nmp._anchor_id__math_dist_quantile_c___quantile_from_the_complement_of_the_probability_
>
> Boy, things sure are hard to find in the boost doc!
> And what's up with these paths?
>
> It might be even better here to use a quantile value like
> 0.95 and then allow multiple tries so that you get a
> false positive test rate per test of 1e-6 or so.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: generated quantities block executed only for saved samples
messages.subject_clean: generated quantities block executed only for saved samples
messages.body_plain:
This post concerns a pretty fundamental language
design decision, so please chime in if you have
an opinion!

On 3/1/13 11:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:

 > Actually, this [print in generated quantities] is not work

> well for Stan during the warmup phase if the warmup sample is not saved.

It's a feature, not a bug :-)

The generated quantities block is only executed for
saved samples.  (It can't affect the parameters sampled.)

In particular, the generated quantities block is not called
during warmup if warmup samples are not saved and it is not
called for thinned samples.

We could change that behavior and call it all the time,
even for samples that aren't saved.

- Bob

On Friday, March 1, 2013 10:14:12 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is there anything else we need (or want) to do for this
> release?

I don't think we should delay v1.2 for this alone, but much of the code in the examples section of the rstan package is wrapped inside a \dontrun block, which means it is not run when a user executes example(foo). The reason for this is that it would take a relatively long time to compile and run a model in order to illustrate the behavior, but it has the downside that the code in the examples section is not actually tested and is generally less useful to the user.

What I do in the mi package is to cache the output of a simple but general model, save it to R/sysdata.rda, and then load it with a comment in the examples section to illustrate the function being documented. The sysdata.rda file is mentioned at

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Package-subdirectories

So, with rstan it would be something like this in R

require(rstan)
dogs <- stan_demo("dogs", save_dso = FALSE)
save(dogs, file = "STAN_HOME/rstan/rstan/R/sysdata.rda", compress = "xz")

then in a shell

git add rstan/rstan/R/sysdata.rda
git commit -m "update sysdata.rda"

then in all the relevant manpages remove the \dontrun braces and insert

dogs <- rstan:::dogs # cache of stan_demo("dogs")

then whatever function is being documented can use this object to illustrate plots, etc.

This works well, but we have to remember to recache every time the format of a stanfit object changes.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 3/1/13 11:27 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> I'll have the rest of the univariate distributions gradients done this weekend. That's the last thing on my list for 1.2
>
> Regarding cdfs, the ones Michael have written have been:
> - unit tested
> - added to the language (function_signatures.hpp)
> - model tested (in src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled)
> - added to the doc

Fantastic progress!

I finally took a look at some of this code and I'm
a bit confused about what's going on with the definitions
and error checking.  Maybe I'm missing something, but I
have the following questions and remaining to-do items.

0.  There are tab chars in the CDF code.  Looks like we need to
script another eradication.   Can everyone verify that the
environment they're using for text gets rid of tabs?  I just
went through mine and it looks like I'm not the culprit this time.

1.  What was the final decision on the domains of the cdfs?
Do they return 0 for values below the support of the density/mass
function and to 1 for values above the support?

2.  In Bernoulli CDF, I see this:

       // Ensure non-zero argument lenghts
       if (!(stan::length(n) && stan::length(theta)))
	return 0.0;

Why return 0?  I'd have thought 1.0 would be a better
boundary condition here if we don't want to raise an
error.  The reason is that it's the appropriate unit to
ground out the recursion because values are multiplied,
not added.

3.  I take it the propto for CDFs are just there to let us
avoid calculating them when we don't want to for truncated models?
That is, if we have

     y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,]

we don't really need to calculate the cdfs.   We should still
calculate the constraints, though.

In practice, for Bernoulli CDF, I see this:

    // Return if everything is constant and only proportionality is required
    if (!include_summand<propto,T_prob>::value)
        return 0.0;

Why 0?  This also seems like it should be 1.0 for the same
reason as above.    As is, I think it will do the wrong thing for
a truncated model, as in:

    y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,];

This would effectively return 0 probability because the
include_summand metaprogram will evaluate to false.

4.  The ones remaining to be coded(?)/tested(?)/documented
     are:

    uniform_cdf             [not that we want to encourage this one for truncation!]
    binomial_logit_cdf
    hypergeometric_cdf      [very low priority]
    ordered_logitistc_cdf
    poisson_log_cdf
    cauchy_cdf
    double_exponential_cdf
    chi_square_cdf
    gamma_cdf

5.  I'd eventually like to get the CDF formulas into the doc along
with their support and formulas.  I'll work on that.
I'd really like to get gradients in for everything.  I think it'll be
a useful general feature of our doc for people implementing other
things directly.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] doc & behavior of CDFs?
messages.body_plain:
> 0.  There are tab chars in the CDF code.  Looks like we need to
> script another eradication.   Can everyone verify that the
> environment they're using for text gets rid of tabs?  I just
> went through mine and it looks like I'm not the culprit this time.

I've been using XCode with explicit space-for-tab settings, but I do see tabs everywhere every time I pull.

> 1.  What was the final decision on the domains of the cdfs?
> Do they return 0 for values below the support of the density/mass
> function and to 1 for values above the support?

Yup, we went for values below/above the proper support as valid but returning 0/1.  This admits distributions with parameter-dependent support, such as the Pareto.

> 2.  In Bernoulli CDF, I see this:
>
>      // Ensure non-zero argument lenghts
>      if (!(stan::length(n) && stan::length(theta)))
> 	return 0.0;
>
> Why return 0?  I'd have thought 1.0 would be a better
> boundary condition here if we don't want to raise an
> error.  The reason is that it's the appropriate unit to
> ground out the recursion because values are multiplied,
> not added.

Random choice -- looking at it now I'd rather throw an error than pass a 1.

> 3.  I take it the propto for CDFs are just there to let us
> avoid calculating them when we don't want to for truncated models?
> That is, if we have
>
>    y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,]
>
> we don't really need to calculate the cdfs.   We should still
> calculate the constraints, though.
>
> In practice, for Bernoulli CDF, I see this:
>
>   // Return if everything is constant and only proportionality is required
>   if (!include_summand<propto,T_prob>::value)
>       return 0.0;
>
> Why 0?  This also seems like it should be 1.0 for the same
> reason as above.    As is, I think it will do the wrong thing for
> a truncated model, as in:
>
>   y ~ normal(0,1) T[0,];
>
> This would effectively return 0 probability because the
> include_summand metaprogram will evaluate to false.

Yeah, I was thinking on the log scale -- log(1) = 0.  It should be returning 1.

> 4.  The ones remaining to be coded(?)/tested(?)/documented
>    are:
>
>   uniform_cdf             [not that we want to encourage this one for truncation!]
>   binomial_logit_cdf
>   hypergeometric_cdf      [very low priority]
>   ordered_logitistc_cdf
>   poisson_log_cdf
>   cauchy_cdf
>   double_exponential_cdf
>   chi_square_cdf
>   gamma_cdf

Cauchy is coded/partially tested.

> 5.  I'd eventually like to get the CDF formulas into the doc along
> with their support and formulas.  I'll work on that.
> I'd really like to get gradients in for everything.  I think it'll be
> a useful general feature of our doc for people implementing other
> things directly.

Heartily agree.  If we decide on a format I can fill in the deets.

messages.subject: JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
There's a boost lib that parses JSON into a
DOM-like property tree:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/doc/html/property_tree.html

We'd just need to implement our data interface on top of
a property tree the same way we have done for reading
from files and reading from the R environment.

I'm less clear on JSON output -- I don't see anything
to write JSON-formatted data, though it's bound to
be a lot easier than parsing if we need to write it
ourselves.  The output needs to come in the form of
headers and then lines of data, and will hopefully be
streamable.

We might literally be able to set a compiled Stan
model up to work as a pipe taking JSON-formatted
data as standard input and producing JSON-formatted
data as standard output with control given by the
command-line options of the compiled Stan model.   With
that, a fully-functional, basic Python interface should
be really simple.

- Bob

We don't actually need to get to or from R at any
point.  RStan is a wrapper around Stan.  We'd
write a PStan wrapper for Python and an MStan wrapper
for MATLAB, all of which would only depend on
Stan's code (which itself so far only depends on
Boost and Eigen libs).

I'd like to do one thing at a time, which in this
case, would be to write JSON input and output
parsers and generators for Stan.  It'll be great it that'll make it
easier to run on clusters (or "in the cloud" as
the people with money like to hear).

We're only interested in integrating software without
copyleft encumbrances, so Avogadro is out.  It's GPL-ed
from what I can see:

   http://wiki.openchemistry.org/Avogadro

But all they seem to be using is jsoncpp.  That site
looks like it's "public domain",

   http://sourceforge.net/projects/jsoncpp/

which is usually what someone puts up who doesn't
understand licensing, see, e.g.,

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain_software

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Trunc_Normal Distribution
messages.body_plain:
That'll be insanely inefficient for truncations
any ways out on the tail.

One general approach to sampling

    v ~ Foo(theta) T[L,H];

if we have cdfs and inverse cdfs is

    u ~ uniform(Foo_cdf(L|theta), Foo_cdf(H|theta));

    v <- Foo_inverse_cdf(u|theta);

This is also pretty inefficient and I'm guessing there will be
much better ways to do this for some specific distributions
and subcases.

Anyway, I still say we punt on this until we use
truncated normals.

- Bob

On 3/4/13 6:08 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Is there ever a situation in Stan where '=' means anything besides "I
> meant to type <-" (or more rarely "I meant to type ==")?

There's the lower and upper bounds.

    real<lower=12,upper=27> x;

Maybe those should've been "<-", as in:

    real<lower<-12, upper<-27>

But that just looks really really ugly, and R used
"=" for properties, and we followed R syntax.

> Should be
> pretty easy to catch, if not.

Conceptually, yes it's easy.  But what it means in practice is
that we have to write a separate parser rule that looks like
an assignment, but with an "=" in place of the '<-', then throw an error when
it matches.  Not too hard.  But when we add more rules, we
immediately break windows and have to break our parser into
more bits, ...

 > (We could even translate it to <- like R
 > does, but I don't want to start a heated discussion on that topic.)

We've had it already and decided on just "<-".

FWIW, I liked "=" instead of "<-" and "double" instead
of "real" so that I don't have such a jarring context switch
going back and forth with C++.  But I also would rather just
have a single symbol.

- Bob

messages.subject: Make for Windows
messages.body_plain:
I finally fixed the makefile under Windows so that we can create executables without having to specify .exe at the end.

That means we can either type:
> make bin/stanc
or
> make bin/stanc.exe

What does this mean? We can simplify our instructions because the Windows targets are now identical to linux and Mac targets. Running the targets still require a backslash, but we can't do anything about that.

The fix was to add a target in the make/os_win makefile with a new target
% : %.exe

I don't know why I didn't think of adding that target before in a place that only gets activated under Windows.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
>> 4 chains: each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1; 2000 iterations saved.

I see how that could be misleading.

How about:

    4 chains, each with iter=2000, warmup=1000, thin=4, draws=250.
    total draws=1000.

I might have said "samples" instead of "draws", but I remember Andrew
not wanting to call MCMC draws "samples" to avoid anyone trying to
interpret them as independent samples.

I don't think this is the place to talk about what's saved/stored
or not.

If we go for timing, it'll have to be different because the
iterations, etc., may be different.   I like how Daniel did
it in the print for the command, which would be something like

    4 chains, iter=(2000,2000,2000,2000), warmup=(1000,1000,1000,1000), thin=(4,4,4,4), draws=(250,250,250,250).
    total draws=1000.

This allows the numbers to be different in each chain, which will arise
if we do timing rather than fixed number of iterations.

Also, we need to think about whether if we do timing, we want to weight
chains by size or equally.  The latter is more conservative and what's in
the doc.  But it doesn't discount slow chains that fail to warm up, so
the entire set of chains will be reported not to have converged.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:

On Feb 28, 2013, at 2:08 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I understand what Andrew wants to do in principle.  (Yes,
> it would be a hash table that maps from parameters to
> sequences of lines of code.  Abstractly, a hash table
> implements a function from one type of object to another.
> A list in R implements such a map from names to values.)
>
> But it's a whole lot harder to literally do what Andrew's
> asking than it sounds.  If Stan were interpreted line-by-line
> it would be more feasible.
>
> For instance, consider this simple coding for regression:
>
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>      real mu;
>      mu <- alpha + beta * x[n];
>      y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>   }
>
> If alpha changes, we need to evaluate this whole thing.
> Ditto beta.  But they only show up on the line with the
> assignment to the local variable mu.

Bob:  The above is not quite what I had in mind.  My proposal is not to _parse_ the code for alpha but rather to change alpha and then _evaluate_ the code and see which lines give different results.  Only the lines that give different results would need to be recomputed during the slice sampling for alpha.  Of course, this will fail under certain settings (such as a function that's equal to alpha for alpha>0 and equal to 0 for alpha<0) but I think it could work pretty well for most models.  Also, we could re-check the eval every 10th or 100th iteration or so, just to check that the "active" lines of code haven't changed.

>
> One angle we could use is our current propto calculations
> which is what lets us compute the log joint efficiently up
> to a constant.  If we could somehow make theta[k] the only
> "variable" from the perspective of our trait metaprograms,
> we'd pretty much get the behavior we wanted for free.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Maybe we can discuss this at the next meeting.  I don't
see how it (Andrew's suggestion below) can work, but he
keeps suggesting it, so I apparently haven't done a very good
job of explaining why I don't think it'll work.

Even if Andrew's suggestion could be made to work, it'll
be very hard to code, because we'd need to literally instrument
every line of generated code somehow, index it to store values,
etc.  We really want to look at expressions, not lines.  And
the lines and expressions have contexts.

a loop is implemented like in BUGS or JAGS by blowing out the graph,

     y[n] ~ normal(0,1);

  y[1] ~ normal(0,1);
  y[2] ~ normal(0,1);

But that's just not how it works.  So we'd have to index the lines
that changed by the loop indices.  These can depend on arbitrary
calculations elsewhere, so it's hard to see how to do this.

messages.subject: local adaptation
messages.body_plain:
I was thinking about local adaptation in HMC again, and I remembered an old covariance estimator proposed by Theil and his coauthors that never really caught on in the literature but has the properties that it is always positive definite (even if columns > rows), depends only on the order statistics, and converges to the usual covariance estimator. Theil literature-reviewed himself in a short paper that can be found here

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=13846554235231786818&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

and then wrote a book about it a couple years later that is in the CU library.

I was thinking that every time the leapfrogger goes, you accumulate a quasi-sample of up to 2 * max_treedepth realizations in the neighborhood of the current parameter vector that could be used to estimate the local covariance with Theil's estimator. Since it only depends on the order statistics, the partial derivatives of that covariance matrix with respect to the parameters are all zero, so the RMHMC equations simplify back to the HMC equations.

So, if you use the previous mass matrix to leapfrog to a new proposal for the parameter vector, calculate a new proposal for the mass matrix via Theil's covariance estimator applied to the leapfrogging footprints, and do a Metropolis acceptance test for both the proposed parameter vector and the proposed mass matrix simultaneously, would you preserve all the properties you need for a Markov chain?

Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
messages.body_plain:
RMHMC only works if the metric is differentiable w.r.t. location,
which it sounds like this covariance estimator isn't. The issue is
that there are implicit updates in the generalized leapfrog integrator
that can't be satisfied otherwise.

But it also sounds like you're proposing using a fixed metric within
each trajectory, which can be done with the explicit leapfrog
integrator. However, unless you add some random perturbation to the
mass matrix you'll have a very hard time maintaining reversibility.
Even if you do, you'll wind up with a Markov chain that has a very
hard time moving between regions with different local covariance
structure, since you'll reject transitions that change the mass matrix
too much.

Detailed-balance-preserving local adaptation is tough.

Matt

> But it also sounds like you're proposing using a fixed metric within

That makes sense that it would be hard to get reversibility of the transitions if the proposed mass matrix were different from the current mass matrix. But what lead me to hope that detailed balance could still be satisfied was the overlap between the proof of detailed balance for HMC in Neal's chapter and Theil's derivation of the maximum entropy density. Neal uses the reversibility of the transitions to show that the volume of little partitions of the parameter space is preserved and then does the Metropolis thing in equation 3.8. Similarly, Theil arrives at that the density that implies that covariance estimator by partitioning up a space and then maximizing the entropy subject to the volume-preserving (and mean-preserving) constraints. So, if volume would be preserved for a fixed mass matrix and both the current and proposed mass matrices were obtained under volume-preserving constraints, I thought that might be an avenue in. But maybe there is a part to Neal's argument that hinges on more than just volume preservation that I missed?

> structure, since you'll reject transitions that change the mass matrix

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
messages.body_plain:
Volume preservation is a soft constraint in an MCMC transition—you can
still adjust for it in the Metropolis correction if you can compute
the determinants of the Jacobians of every transition. (Cf. the recent
Lan et al. paper on Lagrangian Monte Carlo.) But reversibility is a
hard constraint—you can't satisfy detailed balance without it. The
leapfrog integrator is both volume preserving and reversible, which
makes it easy to prove correctness in HMC. (Ditto for the generalized
leapfrog, assuming the fixed-point iterations converge.)

Matt

On Wed, Mar 6, 2013 at 11:43 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
messages.body_plain:
Yup, reversibility is they key reason. It's pretty easy to check that
if you run one leapfrog step, negate the momentum, and run another
leapfrog step you'll wind up back where you started (except with
negative momentum). So likewise, if you run L leapfrog steps, negate
the momentum, and run another L leapfrog steps you'll again wind up
back where you started. So the procedure
1. Run L leapfrog steps with size ε
2. Negate momentum
is reversible in the sense that if you run it twice you wind up in
exactly the state you started in. So if you pretend that that
procedure is a random proposal, and plug that "distribution" (really a
delta) into the Metropolis-Hastings formula, you discover that q(θ',
m' | θ, m) = q(θ, m | θ', m'). If you didn't negate the momentum you
wouldn't have reversibility, and it'd be hard to show correctness.

Of course, in practice we generate a new momentum every iteration. But
that's really an interleaved Gibbs sampling step that's theoretically
separate from the proposal we generated using Hamiltonian dynamics.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
messages.body_plain:
In HMC it doesn't matter if we negate the momentum, but it does matter
that we can. Again, a single HMC iteration consists of two updates,
each of which satisfies detailed balance individually: one Gibbs
update, and one Metropolis update. If the Metropolis update wasn't
valid then the algorithm as a whole wouldn't be valid. And the
Metropolis update isn't valid if you don't negate the momentum.

Consider the following algorithm:
1. Resample momentum
2. Simulate dynamics for L steps, accept/reject based on total energy
3. Simulate dynamics for L steps, negate momentum, accept/reject based
on total energy.
Seems a lot like HMC, right? But it's not valid, because the second
step isn't a reversible proposal--if you ran it twice, there is 0
probability that you'd wind up back where you started. And in fact, it
will give you wrong answers if you use a large enough step size that
you get rejections in step 2.

You could also imagine using an asymmetric kinetic energy function
(though I can't think why you would), and then you really would need
to implement the negation before the accept/reject step. The only
reason we can get away with not doing it is because of the symmetry of
the normal distribution (i.e., Normal(x; μ, Σ) = Normal(-x; μ, Σ)).

Matt

in each iteration.

On Mar 7, 2013, at 12:21 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I was thinking about local adaptation in HMC again, and I remembered an old covariance estimator proposed by Theil and his coauthors that never really caught on in the literature but has the properties that it is always positive definite (even if columns > rows), depends only on the order statistics, and converges to the usual covariance estimator. Theil literature-reviewed himself in a short paper that can be found here
>
> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=13846554235231786818&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33
>
> and then wrote a book about it a couple years later that is in the CU library.
>
> I was thinking that every time the leapfrogger goes, you accumulate a quasi-sample of up to 2 * max_treedepth realizations in the neighborhood of the current parameter vector that could be used to estimate the local covariance with Theil's estimator. Since it only depends on the order statistics, the partial derivatives of that covariance matrix with respect to the parameters are all zero, so the RMHMC equations simplify back to the HMC equations.
>
> So, if you use the previous mass matrix to leapfrog to a new proposal for the parameter vector, calculate a new proposal for the mass matrix via Theil's covariance estimator applied to the leapfrogging footprints, and do a Metropolis acceptance test for both the proposed parameter vector and the proposed mass matrix simultaneously, would you preserve all the properties you need for a Markov chain?
>
> Thanks,
> Ben

messages.subject: Pushed support for unit_vector type
messages.body_plain:
I just pushed support for a new unit_vector type.  I've added unit tests and information in the manual.

I didn't have a real Stan use-case for it, but I had needed to work out all the necessary math for another project recently and figured I might as well add it to Stan.

At any rate, you can now put:

unit_vector[N] dir_vector;

and get a vector with norm of 1.

This uses hyperspherical coordinates and so will suffer from singularities at certain points.  This shouldn't cause a big problem in practice unless people are unlucky.  However, it is theoretically possible and, because of the Jacobian term, certain vectors (namely 1,0,...,0 up to 0,...,0,1,0) cannot be used as an initialization because they are exactly at a singularity.

Let me know if anything crops up.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 6:20 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I just pushed support for a new unit_vector type.  I've added unit tests and information in the manual.
>
> I didn't have a real Stan use-case for it, but I had needed to work out all the necessary math for another project recently and figured I might as well add it to Stan.
>
> At any rate, you can now put:
>
> unit_vector[N] dir_vector;
>
> and get a vector with norm of 1.
>
> This uses hyperspherical coordinates and so will suffer from singularities at certain points.  This shouldn't cause a big problem in practice unless people are unlucky.  However, it is theoretically possible and, because of the Jacobian term, certain vectors (namely 1,0,...,0 up to 0,...,0,1,0) cannot be used as an initialization because they are exactly at a singularity.
>
> Let me know if anything crops up.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

> > I just pushed support for a new unit_vector type.  I've added unit tests and information in the manual.
> >
> > I didn't have a real Stan use-case for it, but I had needed to work out all the necessary math for another project recently and figured I might as well add it to Stan.
> >
> > At any rate, you can now put:
> >
> > unit_vector[N] dir_vector;
> >
> > and get a vector with norm of 1.
> >
> > This uses hyperspherical coordinates and so will suffer from singularities at certain points.  This shouldn't cause a big problem in practice unless people are unlucky.  However, it is theoretically possible and, because of the Jacobian term, certain vectors (namely 1,0,...,0 up to 0,...,0,1,0) cannot be used as an initialization because they are exactly at a singularity.

> > Let me know if anything crops up.

messages.subject: forward sampling RNG in place; need RStan update
messages.subject_clean: forward sampling RNG in place; need RStan update
messages.body_plain:
Now that Peter's implementing the RNGs, I added
the ability to call random number generators in the
generated quantities block of a Stan program.  For
example, to assign x to a unit normal random draw,
the code would be:

   generated quantities {
     real x;
     x <- normal_rng(0,1);
   }

I believe we decided to only allow RNG inside the generated
quantities block, because:

   a.  It doesn't make sense over params because we can't
       take gradients, and

   b.  It's not clear it'd be useful in the transformed data
       block, because transformed data's not saved anywhere.

Is this OK for a design?  If not, now's the time to chime in.

If so, we can add the function signatures for the RNGs, add them
to the doc, and provide some examples.

It should make things like Gaussian process models faster
because we can use direct sampling instead of HMC for sampling-base
dinference.

I haven't enforced that constraint yet, but everything's in
place in the grammar to do so after some plumbing work.

I also needed to pass the random number generator through
the Stan command to the model's write_csv() and write_array() methods,
which are what execute the generated quantities block.  So RStan is
going to need to do the same.

- Bob

This appears to be an RStudio only thing because it overwrites the install.packages function with

> install.packages
function(...) .rs.callAs(name,
                                                             hook,
                                                             original,
                                                             ...)
<environment: 0x3ac9a70>
> .rs.callAs
function(name, f, ...)
{
   # TODO: figure out how to print the args (...) as part of the message

   # run the original function (f). setup condition handlers soley so that
   # we can correctly print the name of the function called in error
   # and warning messages -- otherwise R prints "original(...)"
   withCallingHandlers(tryCatch(f(...),
                                error=function(e)
                                {
                                   cat("Error in ", name, " : ", e$message,
                                       "\n", sep="")
                                }),
                       warning=function(w)
                       {
                          cat("Warning in ", name, " :\n  ",  w$message,
                              "\n", sep="")
                          invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
                       })
}
<environment: 0x374e908>

And I imagine the invokeRestart() explains why it subsequently installs. I would guess it is just a flaky internet connection or flaky server thing.

messages.subject: optimization
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan-dev,

I just pushed a change to make --point_estimate use Nesterov's
accelerated gradient method* instead of Newton's method. Its cost per
iteration is linear in the number of parameters, so now we can fit
point estimates for models with more than 1000 parameters. You can use
--point_estimate_newton if you want Newton's method.

Matt

* It's a lot like conjugate gradient—some descriptive slides are at
http://math.sjtu.edu.cn/faculty/zw2109/course/sp04-2-gradient.pdf. It
is NOT the same as Nesterov's dual averaging method. Or his interior
point method. Nesterov is responsible for a lot of methods.

messages.subject: distribution name query
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

Suppose we have as part of our model
β_n ~ Normal(μ, 1/sqrt(τ))
τ ~ Gamma(a, b).
We can integrate out τ and say
log p(β) = a*log(b) - log(Γ(a)) - 0.5*N*log(2*π) + log(Γ(a + N/2)) -
(a + N/2)*log(b + 0.5*Σ_n (β_n-μ)^2).
Is there a name for that distribution, akin to the beta-binomial or
Dirichlet-multinomial distribution? Inverse-gamma-normal would be the
analogous name, but there's already the normal-inverse-gamma, which is
something else.

I ask because I want to implement this distribution in Stan, and I
don't know what to call it.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
I just pushed a two-part fix to gm/command.

1.  I added the rng as an argument in write_csv in the commands.
Don't know how that went missing after my commit yesterday.

2.  Now I'm getting an issue with the Nesterov optimization constructor.
The problem is that the call in gm/command:

        stan::optimization::NesterovGradient ng(model, params_r, params_i,
                                                 std::cout);

doesn't match the declaration:

       NesterovGradient(stan::model::prob_grad& model,
                        const std::vector<double>& params_r,
                        const std::vector<int>& params_i,
                        double epsilon0 = -1,
                        std::ostream* output_stream = 0) :

You can't omit an intermediate variable and the std::cout needs to
be a pointer.  This worked:

       stan::optimization::NesterovGradient ng(model, params_r, params_i,
                                                 -1.0, &std::cout);

so I pushed the change.  I hope that's what was intended here.

- Bob

> In b01cac1782c3edba7354d900758d53ca89d23cd4, you would want to use Eigen's Cholesky decomposition and use a VectorXd rather than a Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> when the number of columns is one. So, something like
>
> Eigen::VectorXd z(Sigma.cols());
> for(int i = 0; i < sigma.cols(); i++)
>   z(i) = std_normal_rng();
> return mu + Sigma.llt().matrixL() * z;
>
> Same with multi_student_t.
>
> Ben

I didn't read this closely enough.  Let me say again, this
is fantastic progress.

Once they're all done, I can add their specifications to
the function signatures for the model.

(We also want to merge the forward mode auto-dif soon,
because we are planning to use it right away for both
optimization and RM-HMC.  Daniel and I are thinking about
the matrix and probability functions for fvar.)

You can build a beta-binomial directly from a beta and
binomial.  Use the beta to select a chance of success
parameter in [0,1], then plug that into the binomial to
sample the value to return.

The hypergeometric is an anomaly for us because it has
no continuous parameters.  There's the obvious, dumb simulation,
where you just do the draws, but there's probably a better
way to do it.  But it's OK to just skip this one.

For ordered logistic, you need to simulate from the logistic
and then plug in the cut points to determine the output.
To simulate from the logistic, you can simulate u from [0,1]
uniformly and apply logit(u) = log(u) - log(1-u), which is the
inverse cumulative distribution function for the logistic, and
then compare logit(u) to the cutpoints according to the definition.

Now that I think about it, we should have the logistic
distribution in our mix.  I'll add that to the to-do list.
The Gumbel's already on it, so we can do all the binomial link
function distributions :-)

Maybe after the RNGs, you can figure out how to add new
distributions.  It's quite a bit more involved on the
meta-programming side than auto-dif or RNGs, but otherwise
the same kind of calc + coding exercise.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I really like the idea of dumping out an annotated
program.  I've never seen it done before, but it
seems like it'd be a good idea for just about any
programming language.

Maybe it'd be kind of like "show plan" in database
programming -- it would give you a notion of how
the code would play out in practice.

That's the computer science definition of "warning" --
not something illegal, but something that's flagged
because maybe you did it by mistake.   For instance,
we get tons of warnings in Stan models for unused variables
because our code generation isn't as concise as it
could be (usually when you declare a variable and don't use
it, it's a mistake).

One warning I want to work on is declaring a parameter
and then not using it anywhere.  That's usually
a mistake, but not always, because

parameters {
   real<lower=0,upper=1> u;
}
model {}

is a perfectly reasonable uniform(0,1) sampler;  but
usually an unused parameter is a mistake.  We could
flag parameters that didn't show up on the left of
a twiddle (~), and/or ones that weren't used at all.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Vectorizing to accept matrices
messages.body_plain:
On 3/11/13 8:19 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Another reason it can work to declare a parameter and not use it is if you're playing around with a model, adding and removing parameters to see what happens.  In that case it can be convenient to alter the model without going back and cleaning up all the derivations.
>
> Which reminds me:  it would be great to allow something like:
> real a, b, c;
> vector(n) d, e;

I have mixed feelings about this, but it's on the
near-term to-do list.

I find it makes it hard to scan for variables and to
doc what they're for.  It's usually discouraged in programming
language style guides.

I can add it and then just soft-legislate against it in
our style guide, which nobody reads or believes in or
follows, but it'll make me feel better.

What I really do want, though is to

(a) allow declarations mixed in, rather than just
     occurring at the top of a block, and

(b) allow compound declaration/definitions, like

     real sum <- 0;

The motivation for (a) is that it's best to declare
variables near where they're defined, and (b) just
takes this to the logical endpoint of doing both at
the same time.  This is good practice because it
lets you see the type quickly and easily see what
the defined value is, thus avoiding undefined variables.

- Bob

On 3/12/13 6:35 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

 > Bob, are you sure that's correct?

My original post is admittedly confusing.  So let me
try to clarify.

We need both the truncation points AND the parameters to be
constant (but not the variate).

So in

    y ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[L,H];

you don't need the truncation if mu, sigma, L, and H
are all constants.

I used an example from the negative binomial, where
the variate is an int, and can't be a parameter:

           if (!include_summand<propto,T_shape,T_inv_scale>::value)

To make this work properly for truncation, the return should
be 1.0.  For the normal, we need T_y, T_loc, T_scale in
the include_summand.

for CDFs.

So for ordered logistic, did you mean something like this?

    template <class RNG>
    inline int
    ordered_logistic_rng(double eta,
			 const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& c,
			 RNG& rng) {
      using boost::variate_generator;
      using boost::uniform_01;
      variate_generator<RNG&, uniform_01<> >
	uniform01_rng(rng, uniform_01<>());

      int i = 0;
      double u = uniform01_rng();
      double logit = std::log(u) - std::log(1 - u);
      while(i < c.rows() && logit < c(i))
	i++;
      return i+1;
    }

And if so, what about the eta? Shouldn't that be considered in implementing the RNG?

Thanks,
Peter

On Mar 9, 2013, at 5:41 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I didn't read this closely enough.  Let me say again, this
> is fantastic progress.
>
> Once they're all done, I can add their specifications to
> the function signatures for the model.
>
> (We also want to merge the forward mode auto-dif soon,
> because we are planning to use it right away for both
> optimization and RM-HMC.  Daniel and I are thinking about
> the matrix and probability functions for fvar.)
>
> You can build a beta-binomial directly from a beta and
> binomial.  Use the beta to select a chance of success
> parameter in [0,1], then plug that into the binomial to
> sample the value to return.
>
> The hypergeometric is an anomaly for us because it has
> no continuous parameters.  There's the obvious, dumb simulation,
> where you just do the draws, but there's probably a better
> way to do it.  But it's OK to just skip this one.
>
> For ordered logistic, you need to simulate from the logistic
> and then plug in the cut points to determine the output.
> To simulate from the logistic, you can simulate u from [0,1]
> uniformly and apply logit(u) = log(u) - log(1-u), which is the
> inverse cumulative distribution function for the logistic, and
> then compare logit(u) to the cutpoints according to the definition.
>
> Now that I think about it, we should have the logistic
> distribution in our mix.  I'll add that to the to-do list.
> The Gumbel's already on it, so we can do all the binomial link
> function distributions :-)
>

So much for "what if" :-)  But hey, I'm all for throwing
everything out into the world, which is why Stan's open
source and our dev group's out in the open.

One reason we haven't done this is just time.

Also, we're already a bit overwhelmed trying to sort out
all the responses to helping us with Python.

This isn't like a bunch of independent research projects,
because all the code that goes into and around Stan needs
to be fairly tightly integrated.  For instance, anyone dealing with discrete
parameters in any deeper way than option (1) below is going to be down in the
guts of our parser, code generator, and sampler interface, and so has to be
sure not to mess up anything that's there that already works.

Writing a new continuous sampler, like Yuanjun did, only
involves half the battle -- he needed to use all the interfaces
we have, but only really had tight integration with one class.
That is, new continuous samplers can be added pretty modularly
at this point.

Writing some new functions, like Peter's doing, is more isolated
still.  There's nothing to integrate with other than to use
some of our libraries.  He's working on Metropolis now, which is
ramping up to the next level of integration.

If we really want to start recruting more developers,
we're going to need to figure out some process to manage
the design and integration of the various parts.  It's
a qualitatively different game when there are more than two or
three people working on a project and the various pieces can't
be made wholly modular.

Now, to get on the actual answer...

>> We could write a short document with our ideas (various possible approaches and the pluses and minuses of them) and
 >> then maybe someone will go out and solve it.  Or we could try to recruit a Ph.D. student, Columbia
 >> or Harvard stat or Princeton CS. What do you think?

I can summarize pretty quickly with the same info as is
on our TO-DO list:

1.  We use the entire log probability function to compute the
     conditional probability of a discrete parameter up to a proportion, then
     use:

     a.  (adaptive) slice sampling for count (unbounded) parameters

     b.  Gibbs (exact discrete) for categorical (bounded) parameters

     PROS:  very easy to implement
            models look exactly as now, but allow discrete parmaeters

     CONS:  very very inefficient

2.  Same as 1, but we try to find a less computationally
     intensive way to compute the log conditional probability up to
     a proportion

     -- Andrew thinks there may be some way to calculate which parts
        of the code need to be executed

        PROS:  models look like now
        CONS:  we can't figure out how to do it (remember that
                 Stan is Turing complete as a language)

        An extreme approach would be to restrict to BUGS-like directed
        graphical models so we can calculate the Markov blanket

     -- Andrew thinks there may also be some way to annotate which
        parts of the code need to be executed for each conditional

        PROS: ??
        CONS: we can't figure out how to do it;
              users have to learn annotation language;
              makes regular models uglier

3.  Same as 1, but we introduce a new block to define the discrete
     conditional probabilities

     -- PROS:  easy to implement;
               very efficient
     -- CONS:  user has to write discrete model twice;
               user has to caclulate Markov blanket, which if they get
                  wrong, leads to an inconsistent model

     We can mitigate the consistency issue somewhat by imposing checks
     of values up to a proportion, but only for finitely many inputs

4.  Hope someone else is more clever than we are.

> It is certainly an interest in my area, plus a closely related issue of multi modal problems. They are not at all trivial!
>
> At present I am using DREAM-type techniques to do these, in combination with NUTS for the continuous variables.

Is there a paper on how to do ensemble methods like DREAM
for discrete parameters somewhere?

- Bob

DREAMZ is designed for multi modal situations. I can't possibly comment on whether it is a true markov chain or not, but hey, when you are in the dark, you welcome any light there is. A search on Dreamz (rather than Dream) will find a paper.

In a way, discrete is easier than multi modal - you know how far apart the modes are. So if you have a rich enough chain, you should be able to explore all possible discrete cases.

I think multi modal is hard enough for optimization, and is simply a dream (sic) for MCMC.

To put it into context, I am right now (i.e. I am currently running tests on my client's cluster) using it with 60 continuous modifiers and 10 discrete modfifiers, with the discrete taking integer values 1 to 5.

The DREAMZ danger is collapsing onto a single mode/discrete values.

I never looked at tempering schemes, apart from my initial studies, as they were simply too inefficient for me.

messages.subject: Re: Testing RNG
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, March 17, 2013 8:23:20 PM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
> I think I've finished implementing RNG for all of the distributions we have so far except for hypergeometric (can't find an effective way to implement a RNG besides actually simulating) and IKJ Corr/Cov (Ben is doing these).
>
> However, I haven't been able to implement effective tests for multi-student t, inv wishart, and wishart, or beta binom. Does anyone have any ideas?

For multivariate student t, the marginals are univariate t, so you can do a chi-squared test of those. For distributions of positive definite matrices, I think we would want to do a test of a scalar function of all the elements in the random variable, such as the determinant. For Wishart and inverse Wishart, see

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/34165/expected-value-of-the-log-determinant-of-a-wishart-matrix

Ben

>

>
> It should make the refactoring we're about to undertake a lot easier,
> because we can more explicitly control template instantiation.

This sounds good. I wonder if it can be used in combination with Eigen 3.2 (in beta now), whose primary new feature seems to be a Reference to an expression

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1Ref.html

These are intended to reduce temporaries, but it seems like we could also enable_if / disable_if depending on whether T is an Eigen thing.

Ben

P.S. With the Eigen 3.2 beta, almost everything in test-unit fails because it can't compile agrad/matrix.hpp because it can't find an appropriate log function.

Re: Metropolis Algorithm
messages.body_plain:
[back on stan-dev]

The next step would be to make Metropolis callable
from stan/gm/command so that there was a command-line
option to run Metropolis.

So it'd be something like:

   ./executable_model --metrop --epsilon-metrop=0.1

if you wanted to start with a simple independent
normal(0,epsilon) jumping rule.

Once that's working, the next step will be to
do diagonal adaptation, so each parameter has
a jumping distance estimated from the data during warmup.
That needs to be merged in the same way as the adaptive
HMC and NUTS implementations.

Then, a full covariance matrix estimate along the lines
of what Yuanjun did for HMC.

Then we'll have a pretty state of the art Metropolis-Hastings
implementation as part of Stan.

One motivation for this project is to evaluate Metropolis
vs. HMC and NUTS.  Another is to give you (Peter) some
experience writing samplers so that you can take on harder
problems in the future.  You should probably read the MC
and MCMC chapters of the Stan manual if you haven't already,
just to get an idea of how this all gets used downstream.

- Bob

>
>

>

>
>> Yes, something like that.
>>
>> The control is from the outside.  This uses
>> what's called an Iterator in the world
>> of programming patterns (sort of like algorithms,
>> only more vague).
>>
>> An outside program calls next_impl to retrieve
>> samples.  We can use the same control for number
>> of loops as we use for our other commands.
>>
>> So the usage from the outside is like this:
>>
>>   metropolis<RNG> m(...);
>>   for (int i = 0; i < MAX_ITERATIONS; ++i) {
>>      sample = m.next();
>>      ... do something with sample ...
>>   }
>>
>> If you look at stan/gm/command.hpp, you'll see where
>> the other samplers get called like this.
>>
>> - Bob

I think the intention is that a Ref<> can be to anything that inherits from MatrixBase, so Matrix<Scalar, Dynamic, Dynamic>, Matrix<Scalar, Dynamic, 1>, Matrix<Scalar, 1, Dynamic>, a Map<> of a Matrix<> a Block<> of a Matrix<> etc. I haven't figured out yet whether expressions like .transpose() would work. Yeah, unless you are multiplying a matrix by itself, then we should use .noalias() on the left.

messages.subject: how much can we precompile? + privacy
messages.subject_clean: how much can we precompile? + privacy
messages.body_plain:
Topic I
-------

One issue that would be nice to address in this
refactoring is the time it takes to compile user models.

One thing we could do to speed this up is more
agressively precompile our libs.

The most general way to do this is to follow the
pattern set up in the grammars (which was forced
upon us by Windows compiler lameness).

The general idea is for each function foo()
would be to have three separate files:

    foo.hpp   pure header file, included by clients
              who link against the precompile lib

    foo_def.hpp   actual definitions, included by
                  clients who want to use Stan as
                  a header only lib

    foo_inst.cpp  instantiations of the function's templates,
                  compiled into an archive for users to link
                  against;  includes foo_def.hpp

Right now, the boundary between what gets separated
into .hpp and .cpp files seems rather arbitrary.

And yes, Daniel and I decided each function should go in
its own file a la Boost.  It makes it much easier to
limit the scope of dependent includes and also makes the
code files and test files much easier to browse.  They
were getting out of hand.

Topic II
--------

The other issue I do want to tackle is privatization.
We're exposing way too many of the internals of our lib
in the API.

What we want to expose is essentially the functions we
want to doc.  The dividing line for me is in terms of
what functions a client (someone using the Stan C++ library)
might need.

Once we refactor, I'll do a much more thorough job of
doc on the C++ side.  This makes it much easier for a new
developer to jump into the code and also makes it possible
for external clients to use Stan C++ as a library in their
own code.

Daniel's and my focus in doing this has been on the math
and probability libraries for a start, including the
auto-diff.   We think that's the most likely piece of the
whole puzzle to be used as a library.  Next most likely would
be the MCMC and sampling libs and also the model compiler.

Michael's working on refactoring the MCMC lib.

- Bob

P.S.  When the dust settles, I think we'll have Stan 2.0.

P.P.S.  After we fill out the forward-mode auto-diff lib
         and get RM-HMC in, that can be Stan 3.0.  I do not want
         to be forever stuck at 1.x.y versions!

messages.subject: Ref in Eigen 3.2
messages.body_plain:
OK, I think I understand what's going on with Ref.

The only place it will speed things up is if we are
passing expression templates *with contiguous memory*
to Stan functions which then access the members of those
expression templates exactly once (more on this below).

Suppose there's a function foo(m,...) taking a matrix
argument m.  As is, our signature

   return_type
   foo(Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m, ...);

causes an expression template passed in as m to be
evaluated (in Eigen speak) into a temporary Matrix before
being passed by reference.  This requires an allocation
for the temporary Matrix and a data copy, both of which
are relatively expensive.

If we instead define the signature as

    return_type
    foo(const Ref<Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> >& m1, ...);

then passing an expression template to foo() will not
require a temporary allocation to pass the argument.

Whether this will help will depend on how many places we
pass expression templates to Stan functions and how
many times they're accessed in the Stan function.  I'm thinking
that's not many places.  For example, it won't help in the
the generated model code, because we're still going to
have Stan functions return Matrix<...> types, which will
force the allocation/copy.

The one place it would definitely help is in T sum(Matrix<T,...>).

I think it only makes sense to use Ref if we only
access the templates once, at least for agrad::var types.
That's because each use of an agrad::var puts the
operation on the reverse-mode auto-diff stack.
For instance, if we have matrices m1 and m2, and
create the expression template (m1 + m2), then we
really only want to put the element sums, m1[i,j] + m2[i,j], on
the expression stack for auto-dif once.  So if the elements of the
expression template are accessed more than once, it's going to be
more efficient to evaluate it into a temporary.   This is not
the case necessarily with doubles.  Eigen does some template
metaprogramming I don't understand the details of to figure
out when it's best to allocate a temporary.  I'm wondering
if we could get better control of this in general using
traits for Eigen that determine operation costs?  They're
a lot higher for auto-diff var than for double and fvar is
somewhere in between.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Eigen Maps
messages.body_plain:
The problem is that there's no way to create a std::vector<double>
out of a double* without copying the data.  At least not without
a custom allocator.  The underlying issue is that std::vector
wants to manage its own memory.  Here are the constructors:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/vector/vector/vector/

You could use the .data() from a Matrix as an iterator.
With Eigen vectors, you know you'll get the data out in the
proper order.

An Eigen::Map just gives you a view into the data
array.

   std::vector<double> v = ...;
   double* dbl_ptr = &v[0];
   Map<Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> > map_m(dbl_ptr);
   m[1] = 2.0;  // changes v

But as soon as you assign it, you lose the connection:

   Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> m = map_m;  // Copy!
   map_m[1] = 3.0;  // does not change v

You can even customize the stride in the Map in case
you have a 2D array laid out C++ style and you need
to use it in Eigen.  Here's an overview:

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TutorialMapClass.html

- Bob

It doesn't look like a big problem. The class definition

  template<bool used, bool is_vec>
  class DoubleVectorView {
  public:
    DoubleVectorView(size_t /* n */) { }
    double& operator[](size_t /* i */) {
      throw std::runtime_error("used is false. this should never be called");
    }
  };

doesn't allocate any memory, so when the test triggers the std::runtime_error by using false, false as the template parameters and referencing [0], the memory checker barks. Is there any harm to making it like the true, false case?

  template<bool used, bool is_vec>
  class DoubleVectorView {
  private:
    double x_;
  public:
    DoubleVectorView(size_t /* n */) : x_(0.0) { }
    double& operator[](size_t /* i */) {
      throw std::runtime_error("used is false. this should never be called");
    }
  };

Then we run into another problem with MetaTraits.DoubleVectorView_true_true. If I leave uncommented this snippet

  var a_var(1);
  std::vector<var> a_std_vector(3);
  Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> a_vector(4);
  Matrix<var,1,Dynamic> a_row_vector(5);

  DoubleVectorView<true,true> dvv1(length(a_var));
  dvv1[0] = 0.0;
//  dvv1[1] = 1.0;
//  dvv1[2] = 2.0;
  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(0.0, dvv1[0]);
//  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0, dvv1[1]);
//  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0, dvv1[2]);

It barks when it tries to put 1.0 into dvv1[1] given that length(a_var) is 1. I'm not sure where you were headed here.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
All else being equal, fewer gripes are better.

I'm not too worried about warnings for classes
we know are right and can explain why we get false
positive warnings from the compiler.  It'd be
better to fix them, but I don't want to do that at
the cost of using extra memory and an extra constructor
assignment call (the suggested fix below).

I might be able to fix this when I refactor by
specializing more aggressively.   It can be tricky,
though, as the compiler requires the concept to be implemented,
but sometimes we won't use the implementation.

- Bob

In the current release (1.2.0) version, the superclass
prob_grad_ad of the model class implements the log_prob
method for double by calling the virtual log_prob method
declared for agrad::var types.

In the refactored code on the main branch, there's a templated
function that can be used for double or var.

BUT:  The double version won't use the propto calcs, so
the log prob values returned will be different (by a constant
that doesn't depend on the parameter values).

But now that I think about it, I don't know which one will
be called.  There's a non-template virtual in prob_grad_ad:

      virtual double log_prob(std::vector<double>& params_r,
                               std::vector<int>& params_i,
                               std::ostream* output_stream = 0) { ...

and then a template in the generated code for the model class:

     template <typename T>
     T log_prob(std::vector<T>& params_r,
                     std::vector<int>& params_i,
                     std::ostream* output_stream = 0)

The current sampling implementations don't need the double
version.

- Bob

> log_prob() is being hidden away. Should we add lines like "using prob_grad_ad::log_prob;" in our generated code?

Will that still let us use the method template with
specified arguments?

We could also rename the templated function that's
generated and then have the template function called
by log_prob.

 > This
> will unhide log_prob(). In the current generated code, we don't have this problem since log_prob() is defined multiple
> times, but I could see how this could bite us again in the future.

I think this is all too dangerous.  I'd rather rename
to avoid confusion for us and clients.

> Thoughts?

The big issue in my mind is the propto calculations
which currently behave as follows in the templated
code (the first template parameter is propto and
the second is scalar type of parameters):

    log_prob<true,double>  :  always return 0
    log_prob<true,var>     :  drop constant terms
    log_prob<false,double> :  don't drop any terms
    log_prob<false,var>    :  don't drop any terms

We use propto=true to speed up computations.

I think this is really confusing but I don't see any way around
this the way we're currently calculating propto based on
type.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Implementing CDF for SkewNormal
messages.body_plain:
I'm not seeing the definition of owenst on the
fvar branch I just pulled from origin.

But what you probably want to do is follow the rest
of our implementations and write this as:

   {
     using stan::math::owenst;
     return 0.5 * erfc(-(y - mu) / (sqrt(2) * sigma)) - 2.0 * owenst((y - mu) / sigma, alpha);
   }

This will apply stan::math::owenst() if the argument is
a double because owenst is brought into the local namespace.

If the argument is stan::agrad::var, then it'll use
argument-dependent lookup to find the implementation in
the stan::agrad namespace.  Ditto for fvar if you've gotten
around to doing that one, too.

Argument dependent lookup seems mysterious, but it was
designed for exactly this kind of overload:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument-dependent_name_lookup

I'm about to add some refactoring that should make defining
new functions for agrad and fvar easier.

Also, make sure you have all three signatures defined in
agrad:

    var owenst(double,var);
    var owenst(var,double);
    var owenst(var,var);

(I've never even heard of the Owens T function!)

- Bob

messages.subject: mondo refactor roadmap
messages.body_plain:
Just a heads up that Stan's undergoing extensive
remodeling in several of its key libraries.

I'm bringing this up now because Andrew Hunter just
joined us and he'll be initially doing some code review for
us on basic memory management and auto-diff organization with
an eye toward optimization and thread-based concurrency.

Thanks, and welcome, Andrew!

Here's the refactoring plan in play:

1.  math  (ETA:  done, but not yet merged back to master)
Daniel finished the math lib refactoring, including
factoring out tests.  All of the functions are being pulled
into their own files, which makes the testing and
dependencies much clearer.

2.  agrad  (ETA: 1 day)
Daniel's now working on refactoring agrad along the
same lines.  All the specialized vari implementations
will go into the files with the functions where they're
used and the generic ones will get pulled out into their
own files along with specialized function implementations.

3.  mcmc  (ETA:  I forgot to ask Michael)
Michael's refactoring the mcmc package to make the
design more modular in terms of integrators, mass
matrices, and adaptation.

At this point, none of our current functionality will have
changed from a modeling language user perspective, but the underlying
code should be much more manageable.

We could release a Stan version 1.3.0 here.

The next steps will build on the above refactorings.

4.  views for vectorization (ETA: a few days after we start plus distros)
I'm renaming VectorView to sequence_view and generalizing
it to handle arbitrary types as well as scalars so that
it'll work for our mulitivariate probability functions.
I'm going to generalize DoubleVectorView to sequence_container,
because it provides a concrete implementation with its
own memory.

5.  fvar (ETA: 1 day after we start)
Forward-mode auto-diff is ready to bring into the master
branch.  It's only complete for special functions -- no matrix
or probability function implementations yet.

I need to write up standalone doc at this point for the C++
API, because it'll be stable enough to announce.  We've been
holding off in anticipation of this major refactoring.

6. RNG in generated quantities (1 day)
I've already added random-number generation for the generated
quantities block and Peter's been pushing the actual RNGs to
the master branch as they're done and tested.  This is mainly
a documentation and parser error-condition handling effort.
So it'll probably get done earlier.

At this point, we should definitely release 1.3.0 or 1.4.0.

7.  RM-HMC (??)
This is the big project Michael undertook the MCMC
refactorization in order to implement.  In order to support it,
we need to build out the rest of the fvar lib.

With RM-HMC, we'll have Stan 2.0.0.

Then, it'll be time to think about discrete sampling.

- Bob

messages.subject: Memory Error
messages.body_plain:
Can anyone confirm the bug I've spend the last few hours dealing with?  If you pull the hmc_refactor branch and compile/run the example.stan model, it should call unit_metric_hmc:transition a few times on its own, and then finally call it via the warmup -> run_markov_chain functions.  For some reason, when unit_metric_hmc::transition is called in the loop within run_markov_chain, the address of the class instance is changed (but not until after it has returned, as noted by the outputs of "this" at the very beginning and very end of the method).

If you add something like "std::cout << sampler.get_stepsize() << std::endl;" to the beginning of run_markov_chain, before the loop, the problem goes away.  This seems it indicate some kind of stack issue, but I can't find any leaks or overflows.  I get the same behavior for both clang and g++, which would hopefully indicate that there aren't any compiler errors at play.

If anyone is running Linux, a Valgrind diagnostic would be greatly appreciated.

-Mike

On 3/27/13 3:03 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Managing this kind of memory-based state of an object
>> is why the STL uses pointer-to-implementation
>> wrappers for classes like std::vector.  For std::vector,
>> no matter what the client does (at least in a single threaded
>> environment, the underlying storage array is in a good memory

>
> But can this protect against overflow?  I think what was happening here was that some other variable was overflowing into the address of a class, so that the class was not pointing to the correct spot in memory anymore.  I don't even understand the Boost RNG setup enough to fully understand why it overflowed, but at least it's working now.

Sure -- you just need bounds checking.  C++ errs on
the side of speed vs. safety, though, so it's all down
to you.

Boost RNG is pretty straightforward once you understand
what's going to be passed by copy and what's going to
be passed by reference.  You absolutely must pass by
reference if you want to share the base RNG --- otherwise
it copies the state, so you wind up with all these highly
correlated RNGs floating around.

>> Of course, C++ is not a "nanny language" like
>> Java, so it happily lets you call methods that are so
>> unsafe they can segfault.
>
> I'm fine with that -- C++ is very much the Spider-Man of languages.

Spidey's powers are elegant.  And he's witty.

 > With great power comes great responsibility.  And memory checkers.

I had no idea Uncle Ben said that in the first Spiderman.
The quote's apparently been around at least since Voltaire.

It's also what JJ Allaire (author of RStudio) said
about C++ when he was here.

- Bob

>

They should absolutely be configured to work by reference.

> Should we go ahead and make all of the internal storage just references
 > to the external RNG passed as an argument?

Yes!

I just traced through the usage and see the issue
in the base class constructor for HMC samplers:

      hmc_base(stan::model::prob_grad& model,
                const std::vector<double>& params_r,
                const std::vector<int>& params_i,
                double epsilon=-1,
                double epsilon_pm = 0.0,
                bool epsilon_adapt = true,
                double delta = 0.651,
                double gamma = 0.05,
	       BaseRNG rand_int = BaseRNG(std::time(0)))
      : ...
           _rand_uniform_01(_rand_int),
        ...
      { ... }

The variable rand_int should be passed by non-constant reference.
That means we can't have a default value, which means the order of
params needs to change.  We're not using these defaults anywhere, so
no big deal.  (You're probably refactoring all this anyway.)

The declarations of the member variables are OK (note the "&"
after the type, which causes the base to be passed by ref
during construction):

     boost::uniform_01<BaseRNG&> _rand_uniform_01;

The usages within gm/command.hpp also look OK.

- Bob

messages.subject: MCMC/HMC refactor
messages.body_plain:
Michael --- this all looks GREAT.  Way better than the
way the code's currently organized.  All the suggestions
below are very minor.

Michael is using a very different coding style than the
rest of Stan -- how much do we care about this kind of
thing?  I'd volunteer to restyle it, but I don't want to
just do that unilaterally.

Here are some specific comments organized by file.

mcmc/mcmc_base.hpp
------------------
Break this file into two files, mcmc_sampler.hpp and sample.hpp
to follow the class defs.

What's the acceptance statistic and why is it part of a sample?
Isn't acceptance a property of a proposal sample relative to
a previous sample?

I'm ok with using "cont"/"disc" instead of "real"/"int",
but it should be consistent.  (Yes, I realize it's all discrete
floating  point reps underneath for reals, but Andrew 1 didn't
like "double", which is how I originally had it.)

mcmc/hmc_base.hpp
-----------------
Break out ps_point into its own file named ps_point.hpp
We're moving to finer grained and easier to navigate files
in the new math refactor, and I think it's a good idea.

Would it be useful to generalize away from teh normal
distribution for generating momenta?  (I realize a fatter
tailed proposal doesn't help much, but it seems an easy
thing to generalize if it'll ever be needed for eval, etc.)

Looks like you got the RNG refs in there already.

mcmc/hamiltonian.hpp
--------------------
Break out into base_hamiltonian.hpp, unit_e_point.hpp,
and unit_metric.hpp.

What's the purpose of defining templated member functions
outside of the class?  (And I didn't mean that question
rhetorically --- I'm genuinely curious.)

I can see the pain here with the std::vector to Eigen
conversion.  Let's clean all that up next (which should be
a whole heckuva lot easier with this refactor).

What's with the empty comments at the bottom, like "DEFINE
HAMILTONIANS HERE"?

By the time this gets pushed, we should get rid of all commented
out code.

mcmc/chains.hpp
---------------
This doesn't look like it's changed much, but we should get rid of
that block of comments at the bottom.  If they're to-do items,
they should go on the to-do list.

mcmc/adapter.hpp
----------------
stepsize_adapter class to file stepsize_adapter.hpp.  (I'll let
you work out the rest of these moves).

This looks super clean compared to what we had before.

Do you really need setters or could you get away with a rich
constructor?  I'd greatly prefer the latter because it's easier
to reason about the consistency of state with immutable objects.
Then you can get rid of the setters and make the member variables
private.  If you do allow setters, there needs to be a check on
consistent values (such as some of these values being required
to be finite and positive).

mcmc/integrator.hpp
-------------------
Break into files named by class.

You can get rid of the protected: block in leapfrog -- there's
nothing in it.  Ditto the private block of expl_leapfrog.

mcmc/hamiltonian.hpp
--------------------
Break into files named by class.

I think we should avoid mixing the underscore style and camel case,
so I'd rename  "sampleP" to "sample_p" for consistency.  (Overall,
the naming looks great and I take naming very seriously.)

Also some seemingly unanchored comments at the bottom.

mcmc/nuts.hpp
-------------
Break into files named by class.

These implementations look awesome.

In conclusion, I love the refactor.  With this and what Daniel's
doing on the base math classes, this is all going to be a whole
lot easier to understand.

- Bob

I just wanted to ask a question: Is it possible to do the SoftMax thing based on the LDL' decomposition of the Hessian rather than the eigendecomposition? If we think of each "sample" as actually a transition in a Markov chain then the acceptance statistic (acceptance probability in the Metropolis case, tree-sampling probability in the NUTS case) is an important element of the sample.
